title: Olfactory Nerve
purpose: Screen cranial nerve I (olfactory) function: sense of smell (hyposmia = diminished, anosmia = absent).
structure: Olfactory nerve, bulb and tract (purely sensory: detection of non-irritating odours). Peripheral causes: rhinitis, facial trauma, medication; central: olfactory bulb or tract damage.
procedure: Alcohol sniff test (Davidson et al. 1997): patient sitting or standing with eyes closed. Occlude one nostril; hold an opened 70% isopropyl alcohol pad a few centimetres under the nose and ask the patient to identify the smell. Repeat for the other nostril. Some authors use common smells such as coffee or vanilla instead.
positive: Failure to detect or identify the odour on one or both sides.

accuracy.source: none; page states no diagnostic properties are available, clinical value unknown

notes: Part of the 12-page cranial nerve screening series (Damodaran et al. 2014 as the series reference). References: Davidson & Murphy 1997; Cameron & Klein 2010.

title: Optic Nerve
purpose: Screen cranial nerve II (optic): visual acuity, visual fields and the pupillary light reflex.
structure: Optic nerve / visual pathway; afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex. Damage from intracranial hypertension, metabolic disorders, vasculitis, multiple sclerosis.
procedure: Visual acuity: Snellen or LogMAR chart at 6 m or 3 m, each eye separately (other eye covered), glasses or contact lenses worn; if uncorrected acuity is worse than 20/20 (6/6), repeat through a 2 mm pinhole. Visual quadrants: sit facing the patient, who looks into your eyes; place your fingers in each quadrant at about 60 degrees from the meridian and ask which fingers wiggle, or move the fingers diagonally from the periphery to the midline and ask when they appear. Reflex: patient shields between the eyes with a hand; in a dim room shine a flashlight into one pupil and observe direct and consensual constriction; compare sides.
positive: Reduced acuity, a visual field defect, or no pupillary constriction when the affected eye is illuminated while illuminating the other eye gives a normal response.

accuracy.source: Kerr et al. 2010 as cited on the page (not in the reference list)

notes: Source: low sensitivity makes acuity tests a poor screen, yet the best available, so clinical value 'unknown'. ⚠ Kerr et al. (2010) is cited in the text but only Damodaran et al. 2014 is listed in the references.

title: Oculomotor Nerve
purpose: Screen cranial nerve III (oculomotor) together with IV and VI: pupils, accommodation and eye movements.
structure: Oculomotor nerve: medial, superior and inferior rectus, inferior oblique; sphincter pupillae (pupillary constriction); eyelid elevation.
procedure: Pupils: inspect size, shape and symmetry. Pupillary light reflex: shine a light into one eye and look for constriction of that pupil (direct) and the other pupil (consensual). Accommodation: patient looks into the distance, then at the tip of their nose; the pupils should constrict. Eye movements: without moving the head the patient gazes up-right, up-left, right, left, down-right, down-left, or follows a pen in an H pattern; ask about double vision and watch for failure of movement.
positive: Absent light reflex, failure of accommodation, or restricted movement / diplopia in the directions served by CN III.

accuracy.source: none (no accuracy data on the page)

notes: ⚠ The oculomotor, trochlear and abducens pages share one video (wtUBAD--fVI) and the same procedure text; the three nerves are examined together. CN IV moves the eye down and in (towards the nose), CN VI moves it laterally, CN III all other directions.

title: Trochlear Nerve
purpose: Screen cranial nerve IV (trochlear): downward-inward eye movement, examined together with CN III and VI.
structure: Trochlear nerve to the superior oblique muscle (downward gaze towards the nose).
procedure: Same combined examination as for CN III/VI: pupil inspection, pupillary light reflex (direct and consensual), accommodation reflex, then eye movements in six directions (up-right, up-left, right, left, down-right, down-left) or an H pattern following a pen; ask about double vision.
positive: Restricted downward-inward movement or diplopia in that direction.

accuracy.source: none (no accuracy data on the page)

notes: ⚠ Shares the video (wtUBAD--fVI) and procedure text with the oculomotor and abducens pages; the pupil steps described actually test CN III. Cranial nerve series reference: Damodaran et al. 2014.

title: Abducens Nerve
purpose: Screen cranial nerve VI (abducens): horizontal eye movement towards the temple, examined together with CN III and IV.
structure: Abducens nerve to the lateral rectus muscle (abduction of the eye).
procedure: Same combined examination as for CN III/IV: pupil inspection, pupillary light reflex, accommodation reflex, then eye movements in six directions or an H pattern; ask about double vision and check for failure of movement.
positive: Failure of lateral (horizontal) gaze or diplopia on lateral gaze.

accuracy.source: none (no accuracy data on the page)

notes: ⚠ Shares the video (wtUBAD--fVI) and procedure text with the oculomotor and trochlear pages. Cranial nerve series reference: Damodaran et al. 2014.

title: Trigeminal Nerve
purpose: Screen cranial nerve V (trigeminal): facial sensation, corneal reflex, muscles of mastication and jaw reflex.
structure: Ophthalmic division (forehead skin, cornea, conjunctiva), maxillary division (mid-face skin), mandibular division (lower jaw skin; motor to temporalis, masseter, pterygoids).
procedure: Sensory: patient's eyes closed; touch forehead, malar eminence and lower face over the mandible with a cotton wool ball and a blunt pin, asking when touch is felt and whether sharp or dull; compare sides. Corneal reflex: stand to the side, depress the lower eyelid, patient gazes into the distance, touch the cornea gently with a wisp of cotton; ask whether it was felt and observe blinking in both eyes. Motor: patient clenches the jaw while you palpate tone and bulk; patient holds the mouth open while you try to close it. Jaw reflex: index finger on the chin, tap with the reflex hammer.
positive: Sensory loss or side-to-side difference, absent corneal reflex, weakness of jaw closure/opening, or an exaggerated jaw reflex (normal = slight closure or no reflex).

accuracy.source: none (no accuracy data on the page)

notes: Cranial nerve series reference: Damodaran et al. 2014. The jaw reflex is repeated on the facial nerve page.

title: Facial Nerve
purpose: Screen cranial nerve VII (facial): muscles of facial expression, glabellar reflex and jaw reflex; distinguish upper from lower motor neuron facial palsy.
structure: Facial nerve: motor to facial expression muscles (except eyelid elevation, CN III); sensory 'nervus intermedius' to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; reflex functions (corneal, glabellar). Affected e.g. by cerebral infarct or Parkinson's disease.
procedure: Inspect the face for asymmetry (e.g. flattened nasolabial fold). Patient looks up and raises the eyebrows: observe even forehead wrinkling. Patient closes the eyes tightly while you try to open them. Lower face: patient shows teeth, smiles, puffs out the cheeks while you palpate for even tone. Glabellar reflex: patient keeps the eyes wide open while you tap the forehead repeatedly with a finger. Jaw reflex: index finger on the chin, tap with the reflex hammer.
positive: Facial weakness. Upper motor neuron pattern: forehead spared. Lower motor neuron pattern: all ipsilateral facial muscles including the forehead. Glabellar reflex abnormal = repeated blinking on tapping (normal = no blinking). Exaggerated jaw reflex (normal = slight closure or none).

accuracy.source: none (no accuracy data on the page)

notes: ⚠ The page says the corneal reflex was covered 'in our post on the oculomotor nerve'; it is actually described on the trigeminal nerve page. Cranial nerve series reference: Damodaran et al. 2014.

title: Vestibulocochlear Nerve
purpose: Screen cranial nerve VIII (vestibulocochlear): hearing (whisper test, Rinne and Weber tests) and a quick vestibular check.
structure: Vestibulocochlear nerve: cochlear (hearing) and vestibular (balance) divisions.
procedure: Whisper test: patient sitting, cover one ear at a time; at about 60 cm from the open ear whisper a few numbers at the end of exhalation and ask the patient to repeat them; repeat for the other ear. If deficits: Rinne test with a 256 or 512 Hz tuning fork struck and placed on the mastoid process; when the patient no longer hears it, move it in front of the external auditory meatus and ask whether it is still heard (normal: air conduction > bone conduction). Weber test: tuning fork on the middle of the forehead; ask whether it is louder in one ear or in the middle. Vestibular: observe for nystagmus after maximal head turn to one side; more specific tests include the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre (BPPV).
positive: Failure to repeat whispered numbers; Rinne: sound not heard by air conduction after bone conduction has faded; Weber: lateralisation to one ear; nystagmus on head turn.

accuracy.source: Kelly et al. 2018 systematic review (Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg); studies too heterogeneous to pool

notes: Source: clinical value 'at least moderate'. Cranial nerve series reference: Damodaran et al. 2014.

title: Glossopharyngeal Nerve
purpose: Screen cranial nerve IX (glossopharyngeal), examined together with CN X: swallowing, palate and uvula, voice and cough, gag reflex.
structure: Glossopharyngeal nerve (with vagus): tongue and pharynx muscles, thorax and abdominal viscera, larynx.
procedure: Ask the patient to take a sip on command and watch for delay or difficulty swallowing. Patient says 'aah' with the mouth wide open: check that the uvula elevates and the palate is symmetrical. Listen to the voice and cough. Gag reflex: touch the back of the tongue on both sides with a tongue depressor, or the soft palate with a wisp of cotton.
positive: Delayed or difficult swallowing, asymmetric palate or uvula deviation, hoarse voice or 'bovine' cough, absent gag reflex.

accuracy.source: none (no accuracy data on the page)

notes: ⚠ The glossopharyngeal and vagus pages share one video (HG78dKdMyVE) and identical procedure text. Cranial nerve series reference: Damodaran et al. 2014.

title: Vagus Nerve
purpose: Screen cranial nerve X (vagus), the main parasympathetic nerve, examined together with CN IX.
structure: Vagus nerve: pharynx, larynx (vocal cords), soft palate; parasympathetic supply to thorax and abdomen.
procedure: Same combined examination as CN IX: sip of water on command (swallowing), 'aah' with mouth open (uvula elevation, palate symmetry), voice and cough, gag reflex with a tongue depressor on the back of the tongue or cotton on the soft palate.
positive: Hoarse voice or bovine cough (vocal cords fail to close, hollow sound), uvula/palate asymmetry, swallowing difficulty, absent gag reflex.

accuracy.source: none (no accuracy data on the page)

notes: ⚠ Shares the video (HG78dKdMyVE) and text with the glossopharyngeal page. Cranial nerve series reference: Damodaran et al. 2014.

title: Accessory Nerve
purpose: Screen cranial nerve XI (accessory): sternocleidomastoid and upper trapezius strength.
structure: Accessory nerve: cranial roots (functionally identical to the vagus) and spinal roots to sternocleidomastoid and upper trapezius.
procedure: Patient sitting; inspect the neck for atrophy. Upper trapezius: patient shrugs the shoulders and resists you pushing them down. Sternocleidomastoid: patient rotates the head to each side against your resistance.
positive: Atrophy or weakness of shoulder shrug or resisted head rotation.

accuracy.source: none (no accuracy data on the page)

notes: Cranial nerve series reference: Damodaran et al. 2014.

title: Hypoglossal Nerve
purpose: Screen cranial nerve XII (hypoglossal): tongue bulk, protrusion and strength.
structure: Hypoglossal nerve to the tongue muscles (voluntary tongue movement).
procedure: With the mouth open inspect the tongue for atrophy (wrinkling, loss of bulk at the tip and borders). Ask the patient to stick out the tongue and check for deviation. Strength: patient pushes the tongue into the cheek while you press against it from outside.
positive: Atrophy, deviation towards the side of the lesion on protrusion (unilateral palsy), or weakness.

accuracy.source: none (no accuracy data on the page)

notes: Cranial nerve series reference: Damodaran et al. 2014.

title: Hoffmann’s Sign
purpose: Pathological reflex to screen for upper motor neuron (UMN) lesions, e.g. cervical spinal cord compression.
structure: Corticospinal (pyramidal) tract; cervical myelopathy. Also called digital reflex, snapping reflex, Jacobson sign or Trömner sign.
procedure: Patient sitting or standing. Cradle the patient's hand so it is completely relaxed with the fingers partially flexed. Grasp the middle finger proximal to the distal interphalangeal joint and flick the nail of the middle finger with your thumb.
positive: Quick adduction of the thumb and flexion of the index finger.

accuracy.source: Grijalva et al. 2015 (Spine); page text spells it 'Grialwa'

notes: Other UMN screens on the page: Babinski sign, Lhermitte sign. Source typos: 'Grialwa' for Grijalva, 'Trumner' for Trömner, 'the patient isn't sitting or standing position'.

title: Inverted Supinator Sign
purpose: Pathological reflex to screen for upper motor neuron lesions (cervical myelopathy).
structure: Brachioradialis reflex arc (C5-C6) with a cord lesion at that level: diminished brachioradialis response with spread to finger flexors / triceps.
procedure: Patient sitting; support the forearm on your arm so it is relaxed, slightly pronated. Locate the radial styloid at the brachioradialis attachment and apply a quick series of taps near the styloid with a reflex hammer.
positive: Finger flexion or slight elbow extension instead of the normal brachioradialis response.

accuracy.source: Cook et al. 2009 (JOSPT), myelopathy in cervical dysfunction

notes: Weak as a stand-alone test per the source. Kiely et al. 2010 (Spine) evaluated the reflex in asymptomatic people. Other UMN screens: Hoffmann's sign, Lhermitte's sign, Babinski sign.

title: Canadian C-Spine Rules
purpose: Clinical decision rule to safely rule out cervical spine fracture in alert, stable patients after blunt trauma without radiography.
structure: Cervical spine: fracture, dislocation, ligamentous instability.
procedure: Step 1, high-risk factors mandating radiography: age 65 or older; paraesthesia in the extremities; dangerous mechanism (fall from more than 3 feet / 5 stairs; axial load to the head e.g. diving; motor vehicle collision at high speed (over 100 km/h / 60 mph), rollover or ejection; motorised recreational vehicle; bicycle collision). Step 2, low-risk factors that allow safe assessment of range of motion: simple rear-end collision (not pushed into oncoming traffic, hit by bus/truck, high speed or rollover); sitting in the emergency department; ambulatory at any time; delayed onset of neck pain; no midline cervical tenderness. If none applies, refer for radiographs. Step 3: patient actively rotates the neck 45 degrees left and right.
positive: Any high-risk factor, no low-risk factor, or inability to rotate 45 degrees each way = radiography indicated.

accuracy.source: Michaleff et al. 2012 systematic review (CMAJ)

notes: Companion rule: NEXUS criteria. Undetected injuries can lead to spinal cord injury or death.

title: NEXUS criteria
purpose: Clinical criteria to reduce the need for cervical radiographs after blunt trauma.
structure: Cervical spine fracture / clinically important injury.
procedure: Check five criteria (mnemonic NSAID): focal Neurologic deficit (paralysis, paraesthesia, speech/vision/hearing problems); midline Spinal tenderness; Altered level of consciousness; Intoxication; Distracting injury (another serious injury elsewhere).
positive: Any criterion present = imaging recommended.

accuracy.source: Michaleff et al. 2012 systematic review (CMAJ)

notes: Companion rule: Canadian C-Spine rules. References also list Ghelichkhani et al. 2021 (modified Canadian C-spine rule).

title: Elbow Extension Test
purpose: Rule out elbow (olecranon) fracture after acute elbow trauma in adults and children from age 3.
structure: Elbow joint / olecranon.
procedure: Patient seated with both arms exposed and supinated. Flex the shoulders to 90 degrees and fully extend and lock both elbows. Compare injured and uninjured sides visually; equal extension = full extension.
positive: Inability to fully extend the injured elbow = refer for radiography (nearly 50% chance of fracture). Full extension: radiography can be deferred if an olecranon fracture is not suspected; patient returns if symptoms persist beyond 7-10 days.

accuracy.source: Appelboam et al. 2008 (BMJ), multicentre validation

notes: Source: high clinical value to rule out elbow fracture. ⚠ The reference list also includes Jie et al. 2014 ('extension test ... cannot accurately exclude significant injury'), which the page text does not discuss. Lamprakis et al. 2007 also listed.

title: Caradeniz Wrist Rules
purpose: Clinical decision rule to reduce radiographs for suspected distal radius, distal ulna and carpal fractures within 24 h of acute wrist trauma.
structure: Distal radius, distal ulna, carpal bones.
procedure: Five items, in the proposed order: (1) active wrist dorsiflexion; (2) active radial deviation; (3) palpation of the distal ulna; (4) radioulnar drawer test: stabilise the distal radius with the hand dorsum up and apply alternating dorsal-volar stress to the distal ulna; (5) axial compression: hold the metacarpal and compress axially onto the trapezium and scaphoid, then metacarpals 2-5.
positive: Any item provoking pain (for the drawer test also increased movement vs the other side). All five negative = fracture ruled out with 100% confidence in the derivation study.

accuracy.source: Karaca et al. 2016 (Am J Emerg Med), derivation study; not externally validated

notes: Source: moderate clinical value to rule out wrist fracture. Only 39% of ED wrist trauma presentations have a fracture. ⚠ Spelled 'Caradeniz' on the page and in the slug; the reference title is 'Karadeniz wrist rules'. Source typo 'rapezium' (trapezium).

title: Patellar Pubic Percussion Test
purpose: Screen for occult hip (and pelvic) fracture not visible on plain radiographs.
structure: Femur / hip; sound conduction from patella to pubic tubercle.
procedure: Patient supine. Place the bell of a stethoscope on the pubic tubercle lateral to the pubic symphysis on the side to be examined. Tap the patella and listen; compare with the other side. Alternative: a 128 Hz tuning fork on the patella or femoral condyle.
positive: Dull or diminished sound compared with the other side (a distinct sharp sound = negative).

accuracy.source: Reiman et al. 2013 systematic review (Br J Sports Med); Smeets et al. 2018 (n=191, inter-observer reliability 0.7)

notes: Source: high clinical value for hip-related fractures.

title: Fulcrum Test
purpose: Screen to rule out femoral stress fracture.
structure: Femoral shaft.
procedure: Patient sits on the bench leaning back on the hands; stand or kneel on the tested side. Place your forearm under the distal thigh as a fulcrum and press down gently on the dorsum of the thigh with the other hand. If no symptoms, move the forearm more proximally and repeat.
positive: Sharp pain and usually apprehension.

accuracy.source: Reiman et al. 2015 (Br J Sports Med)

notes: Source: moderate clinical value. Companion tibial tests: fulcrum test tibia, hop test (ankle region).

title: Ottawa Ankle Rules
purpose: Clinical prediction rule to exclude fractures of the distal tibia, fibula, 5th metatarsal and navicular after acute ankle trauma and reduce radiographs.
structure: Malleolar zone (posterior edge and tip of lateral and medial malleolus) and midfoot zone (navicular, base of 5th metatarsal).
procedure: (1) Palpate the posterior edge of the lateral and medial malleolus from the tip 6 cm upwards; (2) palpate the navicular and the 5th metatarsal; (3) ask the patient to walk four consecutive steps (limping allowed).
positive: As written on the page: pain on step 1 or 2 and inability to walk 4 consecutive steps = positive (radiography).

accuracy.source: Bachmann et al. 2003 systematic review (BMJ); Dowling et al. 2009 meta-analysis in children also listed

notes: At 15% fracture prevalence a negative rule leaves <1.4% probability of fracture; use should cut unnecessary radiographs by 30-40%. ⚠ The page's positive criterion joins tenderness AND inability to bear weight with 'and', whereas the rule reviewed by Bachmann 2003 uses either finding (bone tenderness OR inability to bear weight) — verify against the original Stiell rule, which the page does not cite. ⚠ The page says a positive rule still means <1 in 3 chance of fracture 'due to the low sensitivity'; given Sn 96.4-99.6% this must mean low specificity.

title: Bernese Ankle Rules
purpose: Alternative clinical prediction rule to the Ottawa ankle rules using indirect stress instead of direct palpation of the injured area.
structure: Ankle and midfoot fractures after inversion trauma.
procedure: (1) Indirect fibular stress: compress the malleolar fork about 10 cm proximal to the fibular tip; (2) direct medial malleolar stress: press the thumb flat on the medial malleolus; (3) compression of midfoot and hindfoot: fix the calcaneus in neutral and apply a sagittal load through the forefoot.
positive: Pain on any of the three steps = radiography indicated.

accuracy.source: Barelds et al. 2017 systematic review with meta-analysis (J Emerg Med)

notes: Source: moderate clinical value for excluding a fracture.

title: Low Risk Ankle Rule
purpose: Decision rule for ankle injuries in children under 16 to separate low-risk injuries (manageable with splinting) from high-risk fractures needing radiography.
structure: Distal fibula and adjacent lateral ligaments vs tibia/medial structures. Low-risk injuries: lateral ankle sprain, non-displaced Salter-Harris I and II fractures, avulsion fractures.
procedure: Examine for tenderness and swelling. Low-risk examination = tenderness and swelling isolated to the distal fibula and/or adjacent lateral ligaments distal to the tibial anterior joint line.
positive: Findings outside the low-risk zone = radiography; low-risk findings = no radiograph needed to exclude a clinically important injury.

accuracy.source: Boutis et al. 2013 (CMAJ); consistent with earlier validation studies

notes: Source: strong clinical value in excluding a fracture. Dayan et al. 2004 also listed.

title: Malleolar Zone Algorithm
purpose: Maximally sensitive prediction rule for high-risk malleolar fractures (tibia, fibula, talus) in children under 18 after a twisting ankle injury.
structure: Lateral and medial malleolus, distal fibula, talus.
procedure: Step 1: tenderness over any part of the lateral or medial malleolus? If no: is the fibula tender just proximal to the malleolus (high risk if yes). If yes: can the child walk 4 steps? Unable = high risk. Able: swelling over the lateral or medial malleolus = high risk.
positive: High-risk pathway reached = radiography.

accuracy.source: Barelds et al. 2017 meta-analysis (J Emerg Med); rule derived by Dayan et al. 2004

notes: Developed because Ottawa ankle rule validation in children gave conflicting results. Source: moderate clinical value.

title: Midfoot Zone Algorithm
purpose: Prediction rule for high-risk midfoot fractures (metatarsal bases, navicular, calcaneus, cuboid, cuneiform) in children under 18 after a twisting ankle injury.
structure: Fifth metatarsal and cuboid.
procedure: Single step: check for tenderness over the fifth metatarsal or the cuboid.
positive: Tenderness present = high risk, radiography indicated.

accuracy.source: Barelds et al. 2017 systematic review (J Emerg Med); rule derived by Dayan et al. 2004

notes: Not yet further validated; source gives moderate clinical value. ⚠ The page says a positive result still means under 1 in 3 chance of fracture 'due to the low sensitivity'; with Sn 95% this must mean low specificity.

title: Tuning Fork Ausculation Test
purpose: Bedside fracture screen using a 128 Hz tuning fork and a stethoscope where imaging is not readily available.
structure: Any long bone; demonstrated on the fibula.
procedure: Expose the limb. Place the stethoscope on a bony prominence proximal to the suspected fracture (over the swelling if present); e.g. fibular head. Strike the tuning fork and place it distal to the suspected fracture, e.g. the tip of the lateral malleolus. Listen for 6-8 seconds and compare with the unaffected limb.
positive: Diminished or absent conducted sound on the injured side.

accuracy.source: Mugunthan et al. 2014 systematic review (BMJ Open); Toney et al. 2016 also listed

notes: Source: moderate clinical value; no conclusion on which bone it works best for. Stress, avulsion and buckle fractures give false negatives because the bone stays intact enough to conduct sound. ⚠ Page title spelled 'Ausculation'.
